$comment: The single source of truth for StingStream's visual language.
Consumed by tailwind.config.js (utility classes) and constants/theme.ts
(typed values for inline styles). Nothing else may hardcode a color, a
radius, a font size or a shadow.
`theme` holds one complete palette per selectable theme: surfaces, text,
the accent triad, state colors, borders, the hover/press overlay, the
scrim and the elevation opacities. Everything outside `theme` is shared by
all three, because it is geometry and timing rather than color.
NativeWind v2 compiles Tailwind at build time and has no CSS variables, so
Tailwind is given the DEFAULT theme statically; the theme a user picks
reaches components through useTheme().colors as an inline style. Run Metro
with -c after editing.
The default. Near-black neutral surfaces, and the StingStream mark's
cyan as the accent. Cyan replaced a teal that was a design-system
default rather than a brand color, and clears AAA on its onAccent ink
(10.4:1) where the old violet could not reach it at all.
Light surfaces, dark ink. The accent is the mark's blue (#0C48FC)
darkened until white clears AAA on it: the artwork blue itself only
reaches 6.3:1. The state colors are darkened for the same reason, and
the overlay is black rather than white -- a white hover wash on a white
card is invisible, which is the bug this token exists to stop.
The logo theme, and the one that has to look least like the default.
Dark and sting share a ground and, at first, shared the cyan accent too --
which made two of the three swatches read as the same theme. So sting takes
the other end of the mark's gradient: violet leads, cyan is demoted to the
focus ring, and the surfaces are pushed further into indigo so the ground
itself is visibly not the default's neutral near-black.
Geometry only. The shadow's opacity is per-theme (`elevationOpacity`):
black at 0.35 under a card is right on near-black and reads as soot on a
light ground.
How a control answers a pointer, a key and a disabled flag.
Overlays are the theme's `overlay` color at these alphas, laid over
whatever surface the control already has, so one pair of numbers covers
every variant on every theme.
A disabled *filled* control fades its fill and its label by different
amounts on purpose: fading the whole thing uniformly leaves a legible
label on an almost-invisible fill, which reads as a link, not a
switched-off button.
